targets.title: The Effects of Music in Advertising on Choice Behavior: A Classical Conditioning Approach
targets.evidence_quote:
Experiment 1 replicated Gorn’s original balanced 2 (prod-

uct: color1 versus color2) £2 (music: liked versus disliked)
design, but used (a) an individual (online) research setting, (b)

contemporary and nonconfounded music and product stimuli,

and (c) a neutral introduction (similar to Kellaris and Cox

1989).
targets.outcome_quote:
Study 1 ﬁnds (weak)

signiﬁcant musical conditioning effects for low-involvement

products. Study 2 fails to ﬁnd effects for higher-involvement

products. Study 3 showed conditioning of general brand and

product evaluations but not of speciﬁc brand-related evaluations.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors present agreement and disagreement across their experiments. Experiment 1 confirms the directional effect but fails their effect-size replication criterion; Experiment 2 rejects the main hypothesis, while Experiment 3 supports general evaluations only. General discussion acknowledges a weak, circumscribed effect and does not state an unconditional overall replication verdict. Earlier replications supply background or materials rather than separate findings directly re-tested.
